paragraphs: It may perhaps be argued that the objects listed in the preceding number ought to be provided for by the State governments, under the direction of the Union. But this would in reality invert the first principle of our political association, since in practice it would transfer the care of the common defense from the federal head to the individual members. Such a scheme would be oppressive to some States, dangerous to all, and ruinous to the Confederacy.

The territories of Britain, Spain, and the Indian nations in our neighborhood do not border on particular States but encircle the Union from Maine to Georgia. The danger, though in different degrees, is therefore common. And the means of guarding against it ought, in the same way, to be the business of common councils and of a common treasury. It happens that some States, because of their location, are more directly exposed. New York is one of these. Under a plan of separate provisions, New York would have to bear the whole weight of the establishments needed for her own immediate safety and for the indirect or ultimate protection of her neighbors. This would be neither fair to New York nor safe for the other States. Various problems would attend such a system. The States that happened to be assigned the support of the necessary establishments would be as little able as willing, for a considerable time to come, to bear the burden of adequate provision. The security of all would thus be subject to the stinginess, improvidence, or inability of a part. Suppose the resources of that part grew more abundant and extensive, and its provisions were enlarged in proportion. The other States would quickly take alarm at seeing the whole military force of the Union in the hands of two or three of its members, and those probably among the most powerful. Each would choose to have some counterweight, and pretexts could easily be contrived. In this situation, military establishments fed by mutual jealousy would tend to swell beyond their natural or proper size, and, being at the separate disposal of the members, they would be instruments for cutting down or destroying the national authority.

Reasons have already been given for supposing that the State governments will all too naturally tend to rivalry with that of the Union, a rivalry founded on the love of power, and that in any contest between the federal head and one of its members the people will be most inclined to side with their local government. Suppose that, on top of this immense advantage, the ambition of the members were stimulated by their separate and independent possession of military forces. That would give them too strong a temptation, and too great a facility, to make attempts on the constitutional authority of the Union and finally to overthrow it. On the other hand, the liberty of the people would be less safe in this state of things than in one that left the national forces in the hands of the national government. To the extent that an army may be considered a dangerous weapon of power, it had better be in the hands the people are most likely to be jealous of than in those they are least likely to be jealous of. For it is a truth, attested by the experience of ages, that the people are always in the most danger when the means of injuring their rights are in the possession of those they suspect least.

The framers of the existing Confederation, fully aware of the danger to the Union from the States' separate possession of military forces, have expressly prohibited them from having either ships or troops without the consent of Congress. The truth is that a federal government and military establishments under State authority are no less at odds with each other than an adequate supply of the federal treasury is with the system of quotas and requisitions.

There are other lights, besides those already noticed, in which the impropriety of restraints on the discretion of the national legislature will be equally plain. The aim of the objection I have mentioned is to rule out standing armies in time of peace. Yet we have never been told how far the prohibition is meant to extend, whether to raising armies as well as to KEEPING THEM UP in a season of tranquillity, or not. If it is confined to the latter, it will have no precise meaning and will not achieve its intended purpose. When armies have once been raised, what shall be called "keeping them up" contrary to the sense of the Constitution? What length of time will be required to establish the violation? Shall it be a week, a month, a year? Or shall we say they may be continued as long as the danger that caused them to be raised continues? This would be to admit that they might be kept up IN TIME OF PEACE, against threatening or impending danger, which would at once depart from the literal meaning of the prohibition and introduce a wide latitude of interpretation. Who shall judge whether the danger continues? This must undoubtedly be left to the national government, and the matter would then come down to this: to provide against apprehended danger, the national government might in the first instance raise troops, and might afterwards keep them on foot as long as it supposed the peace or safety of the community to be in any degree of jeopardy. It is easy to see that so broad a discretion would leave ample room for evading the force of the provision.

The supposed usefulness of a provision of this kind can be founded only on the supposed probability, or at least possibility, of a combination between the executive and the legislative in some scheme of usurpation. Should this ever happen, how easy it would be to fabricate pretexts of approaching danger! Indian hostilities, stirred up by Spain or Britain, would always be at hand. Provocations to produce the desired appearances might even be given to some foreign power, and then soothed again by timely concessions. If we can reasonably suppose such a combination to have been formed, and the enterprise to be justified by a sufficient prospect of success, then the army, once raised, from whatever cause or on whatever pretext, may be used to carry out the plan.

Suppose that, to prevent this consequence, it were resolved to extend the prohibition to the RAISING of armies in time of peace. The United States would then present the most extraordinary spectacle the world has yet seen: a nation made incapable by its Constitution of preparing for defense before it was actually invaded. Since the ceremony of a formal declaration of war has lately fallen into disuse, we would have to wait for the presence of an enemy within our territories as the legal warrant for the government to begin levying men for the protection of the State. We must receive the blow before we could even prepare to return it. All that kind of policy by which nations anticipate distant danger and meet the gathering storm must be avoided, as contrary to the true maxims of a free government. We must expose our property and liberty to the mercy of foreign invaders, and invite them by our weakness to seize a naked and defenseless prey, because we are afraid that rulers created by our choice and dependent on our will might endanger that liberty by abusing the means necessary to its preservation.

At this point I expect we will be told that the country's natural bulwark is its militia, and that the militia would always be enough for the national defense. In substance, this doctrine nearly cost us our independence, and it cost the United States millions that could have been saved. The lessons of our own experience that forbid relying on the militia in this way are too fresh for us to be taken in by the suggestion. Only a force of the same regular, disciplined kind can successfully carry on the sustained operations of war against a regular and disciplined army. Considerations of economy, no less than of stability and vigor, confirm this. In the recent war the American militia, by their valor on many occasions, raised eternal monuments to their fame. Yet the bravest of them feel and know that the liberty of their country could not have been won by their efforts alone, however great and valuable those efforts were. War, like most other things, is a science, and it is learned and perfected only through diligence, perseverance, time, and practice.

Any policy that does violence to the natural and well-known course of human affairs defeats itself. Pennsylvania offers an example of this right now. Her Bill of Rights declares that standing armies are dangerous to liberty and ought not to be kept up in time of peace. Yet in a time of profound peace, because of local disorders in one or two of her counties, Pennsylvania has resolved to raise a body of troops, and she will in all probability keep them up as long as the public peace appears to be in any danger. Massachusetts offers a lesson on the same subject, though on different ground. That State was compelled to raise troops to put down a domestic insurrection, and she did so without waiting for the approval of Congress that the Articles of Confederation require. She still keeps a corps in pay to prevent the spirit of revolt from reviving. The particular constitution of Massachusetts put no obstacle in the way of this measure. But the case still teaches us that situations are likely to arise under our government, as under those of other nations, in which a military force in time of peace will sometimes be essential to the security of society, and that it is therefore improper in this respect to control the legislature's discretion. Applied to the United States, it also shows how little the rights of a weak government are likely to be respected, even by its own constituents. And it shows us, besides, how poorly matched parchment provisions are against public necessity.

It was a fundamental maxim of the Lacedaemonian commonwealth that the post of admiral should not be given twice to the same person. The Peloponnesian allies, having suffered a severe defeat at sea by the Athenians, demanded Lysander, who had earlier served successfully in that capacity, to command the combined fleets. The Lacedaemonians, to please their allies and yet keep up the appearance of adhering to their ancient institutions, resorted to the flimsy subterfuge of giving Lysander the real power of admiral under the nominal title of vice-admiral. This instance is chosen from a multitude that might be cited to confirm the truth already stated and illustrated by examples from our own country: that nations pay little regard to rules and maxims that by their very nature run counter to the necessities of society. Wise politicians will be cautious about fettering the government with restrictions that cannot be observed. They know that every breach of the fundamental laws, though dictated by necessity, impairs the sacred reverence that rulers ought to feel toward the constitution of a country, and creates a precedent for other breaches where the same plea of necessity does not exist at all, or is less urgent and obvious.
